theory.title: Arrays and invariants
theory.explanation: An array gives indexed access. A useful invariant states what the processed prefix already guarantees. Separate reading and writing positions when compacting in place. Sorting may simplify a problem but changes order and costs time.
theory.workedExample: To compact [0,4,0,7], a write pointer advances only for nonzero values: [4,7,…]. Fill the remaining suffix with zeroes.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Hash maps and counting
theory.explanation: Hash maps exchange additional memory for avoiding repeated scans. Keys must encode exactly the equivalence relation you need. Average constant-time operations do not make an algorithm constant-space.
theory.workedExample: For anagrams, the sorted characters in eat and tea form the same key aet; each key stores a group.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Two pointers
theory.explanation: Two-pointer methods discard candidates using an ordering argument. Always explain why moving a boundary cannot discard a better answer. Some require sorted input; do not silently sort when original indices matter.
theory.workedExample: For sorted [1,3,5,8] and target 9, 1+8 is already a match; if too small, only increasing the left value can help.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Sliding windows
theory.explanation: A window tracks a contiguous region and a summary that supports adding/removing an endpoint. Variable windows need a monotonic validity condition; negative numbers often break positive-sum shrinking arguments.
theory.workedExample: For positive numbers and target 7, expand until sum ≥7, record length, then shrink while the condition remains true.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Prefix sums and differences
theory.explanation: A prefix aggregate turns a repeated range calculation into a subtraction. Difference arrays invert that idea: store boundary changes, then reconstruct values with a running sum. Indices and inclusive endpoints need explicit conventions.
theory.workedExample: With P[0]=0 and P[i+1]=P[i]+a[i], the inclusive sum l..r is P[r+1]-P[l].
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Binary search
theory.explanation: Binary search works on a sorted space or a monotonic predicate, not necessarily an array. Define the interval convention and a loop variant that strictly decreases. Overflow-safe midpoint formulas matter in fixed-width languages.
theory.workedExample: For first true, keep a half-open [lo,hi) range. A true midpoint moves hi to mid; false moves lo to mid+1.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Stacks and monotonic stacks
theory.explanation: A stack models nested or last-in-first-out work. A monotonic stack additionally preserves sorted candidates; removed elements are proved irrelevant or receive their final answer. Store indices when distance or expiration matters.
theory.workedExample: In temperatures [70,72], 72 resolves the unanswered index of 70, giving a wait of one day.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Linked lists
theory.explanation: Linked lists trade random access for cheap link edits when the relevant node is known. Draw references before changing them. Dummy nodes simplify operations that may replace the head. Pointer algorithms must account for cycles.
theory.workedExample: To reverse one link, save next, point current.next to previous, then advance previous and current.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Binary tree traversal
theory.explanation: Tree recursion needs a clear meaning for one call’s result. Depth-first traversal uses the call stack; breadth-first traversal exposes levels. Work is usually O(n), but memory depends on height or width.
theory.workedExample: For height, null returns zero and a node returns 1+max(leftHeight,rightHeight). A skewed tree has height n.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: BSTs and ordered structures
theory.explanation: A binary search tree orders every descendant, not only immediate children. Inorder traversal yields sorted values under a strict ordering convention. Balanced trees give logarithmic height; arbitrary BSTs can degrade to chains.
theory.workedExample: A node in the right subtree of 10 must remain above 10 even when its immediate parent is 15.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Heaps and selection
theory.explanation: A heap exposes one extreme efficiently without fully sorting all items. For top-k retention, the root should be the least useful retained candidate. State whether duplicates count and whether order matters in the output.
theory.workedExample: To retain the three largest numbers, a min-heap of size three removes the smallest retained number after a better arrival.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Backtracking and search spaces
theory.explanation: Backtracking constructs a partial answer, explores a choice, then undoes it. Pruning requires a proof that no valid completion remains. Copy completed mutable paths; otherwise later changes corrupt earlier results.
theory.workedExample: For subsets of [a,b], branch include/exclude for a then b; output size itself is exponential.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Graph traversal
theory.explanation: A graph model states what nodes and edges mean. Visited marking prevents redundant work and cycles. BFS gives fewest edges in unweighted graphs; DFS provides reachability and component structure.
theory.workedExample: An undirected graph with edges 0–1 and isolated 2 has two components; a scan must start a traversal from every unvisited node.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Graph ordering and connectivity
theory.explanation: Directed dependencies need cycle-aware ordering. Weighted paths need algorithms matching weight constraints. Union-find maintains evolving undirected components but does not itself recover arbitrary shortest paths.
theory.workedExample: Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly removes a zero-indegree node; if fewer than V nodes are removed, a directed cycle remains.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Dynamic programming foundations
theory.explanation: Define the state before the recurrence. A state summarizes everything from the past needed to choose the future. Base cases and evaluation order are part of correctness, not initialization trivia.
theory.workedExample: For house robbery, best[i]=max(best[i-1],value[i]+best[i-2]); the second choice skips the adjacent house.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Sequence and grid DP
theory.explanation: Two-dimensional DP often compares prefixes of two sequences or paths into a grid cell. State size determines memory; rolling rows work only when no later transition needs discarded values.
theory.workedExample: LCS on prefixes uses 1+diagonal for equal characters; otherwise the better of dropping either final character.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Greedy strategies and intervals
theory.explanation: A greedy choice must be supported by an exchange argument or invariant. Choosing locally best without proof is a heuristic. Intervals require explicit endpoint overlap semantics.
theory.workedExample: For maximum nonoverlapping meetings, an earliest finishing meeting leaves at least as much room as any alternative first choice.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Strings and tries
theory.explanation: String algorithms must declare the character model: these exercises use ASCII unless noted. A trie shares prefixes, making prefix queries natural. Repeated string concatenation may add costs hidden by high-level syntax.
theory.workedExample: A trie containing car and cat shares c→a, then branches into r and t; terminal markers distinguish a word from a prefix.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Bits, arithmetic and numeric models
theory.explanation: Bit operations act on a fixed-width representation; JavaScript bitwise operators use signed 32-bit integers. Choose BigInt or another representation when constraints exceed it. Arithmetic algorithms also need an overflow and rounding model.
theory.workedExample: XOR cancels equal operands: a XOR a = 0. Thus XOR of [4,1,4] leaves 1 when every other value appears twice.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: Data-structure design
theory.explanation: A data-structure design starts with a precise operation contract, invariants, and cost targets. Combine structures only when each pays for a required operation. Trace multi-operation sequences including updates and eviction.
theory.workedExample: An LRU combines a key→node map with a doubly linked recency list: lookup finds the node, list edits move or evict it in constant time.
theory.pitfalls: Account for empty input, duplicate values, mutation and auxiliary space. Test your implementation; a familiar pattern is not a proof.

theory.title: JavaScript language
theory.explanation: JavaScript uses lexical scope and first-class functions. Primitive values and object references behave differently under copying and equality. Coercion follows operator-specific rules. A reliable explanation predicts an observable result and then distinguishes the language rule from coding convention.
theory.workedExample: A spread of {settings:{dark:false}} copies only the outer object; mutating copied.settings.dark changes the shared nested object.
theory.pitfalls: Do not describe closures as frozen copies of values or claim const makes objects immutable.

theory.title: Async JavaScript
theory.explanation: The event loop coordinates synchronous work and queued callbacks. A Promise represents a future settlement, not a thread. Correct async code handles rejection, ordering, cancellation, cleanup, and concurrency limits. Scheduling details differ between browser and Node contexts.
theory.workedExample: If request A starts first but finishes after request B, the UI must discard A when B represents the current query.
theory.pitfalls: Async functions can still block on CPU loops. A timeout is not a guarantee that the underlying work stopped.

theory.title: TypeScript and contracts
theory.explanation: TypeScript checks programs statically and erases most types at runtime. Model states with unions, validate unknown external data, and keep generics tied to real relationships. A type assertion is a claim made by the programmer, not a parser.
theory.workedExample: A union {status:"loading"} or {status:"success",data:User} makes data access conditional on a status check.
theory.pitfalls: Avoid any at untrusted boundaries and avoid asserting away an error without checking runtime data.

theory.title: React state and lifecycle
theory.explanation: React renders a snapshot of props and state, then commits changes. State should describe the minimum authoritative facts; derived values can often be calculated during render. Effects synchronize with external systems and need symmetric cleanup.
theory.workedExample: Three setCount(count+1) calls read the same snapshot. Three functional updates can compose into three increments.
theory.pitfalls: Do not use effects to mirror every prop into state or mutate state objects in place.

theory.title: React performance and accessible UI
theory.explanation: Performance and accessibility are user-observable properties. Measure a slow journey before optimizing. Accessible controls need names, keyboard operation, focus management, and meaningful status messages. A fast screen that hides errors is not a complete feature.
theory.workedExample: A form failure should preserve entered values, show field-specific messages, and focus the error summary or first invalid field.
theory.pitfalls: Memoization is not a substitute for measuring network, database, or rendering cost.

theory.title: Next.js application boundaries
theory.explanation: Next.js combines server and client rendering capabilities. Choose a boundary based on data access and interactivity, and verify caching behavior against the installed version. Rendering strategy is separate from access control. Static export cannot supply runtime server endpoints.
theory.workedExample: A server component can fetch private data and pass a safe serializable result to a small client filter, without shipping the secret.
theory.pitfalls: Do not assume all caching defaults from an older Next.js version still apply.

theory.title: Node.js runtime
theory.explanation: Node coordinates JavaScript execution with event-loop scheduling and asynchronous facilities. I/O concurrency does not remove CPU bottlenecks. Streams control memory and backpressure; process lifecycle must include shutdown and error reporting.
theory.workedExample: Reading a huge file into one buffer costs memory proportional to the file; a stream can process bounded chunks while respecting consumer speed.
theory.pitfalls: Do not call a CPU loop nonblocking merely because its wrapper is async.

theory.title: API design and security
theory.explanation: An API contract defines inputs, outputs, errors, identity, and allowed state transitions. Validation is required at the boundary regardless of UI checks. Authentication identifies a caller; authorization constrains each resource operation.
theory.workedExample: A request for /applications/other-user-id must be scoped by authenticated owner identity, even if the UI never shows that link.
theory.pitfalls: Do not pass arbitrary request objects directly into database filters or trust unguessable IDs as permissions.

theory.title: MongoDB data modeling
theory.explanation: MongoDB documents should follow access and update patterns. Embedding can keep a bounded aggregate together; references support independent growth and access. Indexes accelerate specific queries but consume storage and write work.
theory.workedExample: For per-user applications filtered by stage and sorted by creation time, evaluate a compound index matching that query rather than indexing stage alone.
theory.pitfalls: Do not let arrays grow without limits or assume all joins disappear in a document database.

theory.title: PostgreSQL and Supabase
theory.explanation: Relational integrity belongs in constraints as well as application code. Transactions provide atomic grouping, while isolation determines interactions between concurrent work. Supabase adds client APIs and identity integration; RLS still needs explicit, tested ownership policies.
theory.workedExample: A unique (user_id,idempotency_key) constraint prevents two simultaneous identical operations from both creating new records.
theory.pitfalls: A transaction does not automatically fix every race. A public client key is safe only with appropriate access policies.

theory.title: Python language
theory.explanation: Python’s object model distinguishes names from objects and mutable from immutable values. Iterators support incremental processing; generators suspend and resume execution. Type hints aid tooling but do not generally enforce runtime values by themselves.
theory.workedExample: A default list argument is created once at function definition time; use None and create a fresh list inside when independent calls need independent state.
theory.pitfalls: Avoid hiding failures with broad exception swallowing or assuming every comprehension improves readability.

theory.title: FastAPI and Python services
theory.explanation: FastAPI maps typed request contracts to parsing and validation, but business invariants and authorization remain application responsibilities. Manage database sessions and background work with explicit lifetimes. Async routes help only when their work cooperates with the event loop.
theory.workedExample: A CSV preview can report accepted rows and row-numbered errors without writing anything; commit is a separate, idempotent operation.
theory.pitfalls: Do not treat validation models as authorization or assume an in-process background task is a durable queue.

theory.title: Object-oriented design
theory.explanation: OOP groups state and behavior behind responsibilities and contracts. Encapsulation protects invariants; polymorphism allows substitutable implementations. Inheritance is one tool, not a requirement for every design. Favor changes that reduce coupling and make behavior testable.
theory.workedExample: A PaymentGateway interface can have fake and real implementations; an order service depends on the capability instead of constructing a vendor client internally.
theory.pitfalls: Avoid inheritance solely for code reuse and avoid abstract factories that solve no actual variation.

theory.title: Functional and procedural design
theory.explanation: Functional design emphasizes explicit inputs, outputs and limited side effects. Procedural code can be clear when the workflow is simple and state ownership is explicit. Compare approaches by change patterns and testability, not by treating one paradigm as universally superior.
theory.workedExample: A pure calculateTotal(items,discount) returns a result; a separate boundary loads items and persists an order, making arithmetic independently testable.
theory.pitfalls: Immutability does not remove the need for database concurrency control, and functions can still hide global dependencies.

theory.title: Networking and operating systems
theory.explanation: An HTTP request depends on several lower layers. DNS, transport, TLS and application status are distinct failure boundaries. Processes and threads manage execution resources; memory, scheduling and file descriptors constrain service behavior.
theory.workedExample: A DNS lookup failure happens before an HTTP status exists; a 500 response means an HTTP server was reached and responded.
theory.pitfalls: Do not equate an open port with a healthy application or a connection timeout with a specific root cause.

theory.title: Testing, Git and debugging
theory.explanation: Tests should prove observable behavior at the right boundary. Unit, integration and end-to-end checks answer different questions. Debugging proceeds from reproduction and evidence. Git history supports small, understandable and reversible changes.
theory.workedExample: A failed-save test should verify that text remains available and a retry is possible, not merely that an internal setter was called.
theory.pitfalls: Avoid tests that mirror implementation or mocks that remove the behavior the test claims to verify.

theory.title: Docker and CI/CD
theory.explanation: Delivery pipelines convert a known source revision into a tested artifact and a controlled release. Containers package runtime dependencies but do not automatically make an application secure or reliable. Separate build-time public configuration from runtime secrets.
theory.workedExample: A pipeline installs from a lockfile, runs checks, builds once, deploys that artifact, verifies health and retains a rollback target.
theory.pitfalls: Do not treat a successful process start as readiness or rebuild an untracked different artifact for each promotion.

theory.title: AWS fundamentals
theory.explanation: Cloud architecture combines identity, networking, compute, storage and operations. Each service choice has cost and failure implications. Use least privilege, define resource lifetimes, and verify cleanup; a budget alert is not a hard spending cap.
theory.workedExample: Private resume objects can be accessed through short-lived signed URLs after application authorization, without making the bucket public.
theory.pitfalls: Do not infer AWS IAM permission from network reachability or assume stopped compute means all related costs stop.

theory.title: Distributed-system reasoning
theory.explanation: Distributed systems make delay, partial failure and concurrent views normal. Specify the guarantee per operation before selecting caches, replicas or queues. Prefer a simple architecture that satisfies requirements and identify its next bottleneck with evidence.
theory.workedExample: A lost response after a successful write creates ambiguity: the retry must use the same operation identity to avoid duplicate side effects.
theory.pitfalls: Eventual consistency is not always preferable, and real services should not claim absolute delivery or zero failure without precise assumptions.

theory.title: Interview communication and career
theory.explanation: A credible interview answer connects a concrete situation, your responsibility, your actions and observed outcomes. State uncertainty and ownership honestly. Behavioral practice is about clear evidence and judgment, not memorizing exaggerated claims.
theory.workedExample: For an incident, explain the impact, the diagnostic evidence you collected, the recovery action you owned, and the preventive change you helped deliver.
theory.pitfalls: Never invent metrics, company questions, or production experience. Separate a practice project from professional work.

theory.title: SQL selection and expressions
theory.explanation: A SELECT describes the desired result. WHERE keeps rows for which the predicate is true; SQL NULL introduces unknown rather than ordinary equality. ORDER BY is required for a guaranteed presentation order. Use explicit columns and stable tie breakers.
theory.workedExample: SELECT id,total FROM orders WHERE total >= 100 ORDER BY total DESC,id; returns a predictable two-column result.
theory.pitfalls: Use the downloadable PostgreSQL practice schema, not your live training tables. Declare timestamp timezone and tie behavior; do not assume a join preserves row count.

theory.title: SQL joins and cardinality
theory.explanation: A join combines matching rows; one-to-many relationships multiply output. Choose the result grain first, then aggregate at that grain. A left join preserves unmatched left rows only until later filters potentially remove them.
theory.workedExample: To include users with zero orders, LEFT JOIN orders and COUNT(orders.id), not COUNT(*), grouped by user identity.
theory.pitfalls: Use the downloadable PostgreSQL practice schema, not your live training tables. Declare timestamp timezone and tie behavior; do not assume a join preserves row count.

theory.title: SQL aggregation
theory.explanation: Grouping collapses input rows into groups. COUNT, SUM and AVG differ in NULL handling and empty-set behavior. Distinct counts should reflect entity identity, not hide an incorrect join. Filter rows before aggregation and groups after.
theory.workedExample: A department average ignores NULL salaries; a department with no salary values has a NULL average rather than zero.
theory.pitfalls: Use the downloadable PostgreSQL practice schema, not your live training tables. Declare timestamp timezone and tie behavior; do not assume a join preserves row count.

theory.title: Subqueries and CTEs
theory.explanation: A subquery expresses a dependent or independent intermediate result. EXISTS asks whether any row qualifies and avoids unnecessary result multiplication. CTEs name stages for clarity; do not assume they always improve performance or always materialize.
theory.workedExample: NOT EXISTS is often clearer than NOT IN when the compared set could contain NULL, because NULL can make NOT IN unknown.
theory.pitfalls: Use the downloadable PostgreSQL practice schema, not your live training tables. Declare timestamp timezone and tie behavior; do not assume a join preserves row count.

theory.title: Window functions
theory.explanation: Window functions compute across a related row set while preserving each row. PARTITION BY defines independent groups; ORDER BY and the frame define the calculation’s scope. Default frames can surprise cumulative calculations when ordering values tie.
theory.workedExample: SUM(total) OVER(PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) gives an explicit running total.
theory.pitfalls: Use the downloadable PostgreSQL practice schema, not your live training tables. Declare timestamp timezone and tie behavior; do not assume a join preserves row count.

theory.title: Time-series SQL
theory.explanation: Reporting timestamps require an explicit timezone and interval convention. Missing calendar dates are missing rows, not implicit zeroes. Cohorts, retention and sessions need precise event definitions and denominators.
theory.workedExample: Generate a UTC date series, left join daily aggregates, and COALESCE missing counts to zero before computing a moving average.
theory.pitfalls: Use the downloadable PostgreSQL practice schema, not your live training tables. Declare timestamp timezone and tie behavior; do not assume a join preserves row count.

theory.title: SQL writes and constraints
theory.explanation: Writes should preserve invariants under concurrency. Prefer constraints for shared facts, parameterized values for safety, and transactions for related changes. Practice destructive statements only against the supplied disposable schema and inspect affected rows.
theory.workedExample: UPDATE products SET stock=stock-2 WHERE id=1 AND stock>=2 RETURNING stock atomically reserves only when enough stock remains.
theory.pitfalls: Use the downloadable PostgreSQL practice schema, not your live training tables. Declare timestamp timezone and tie behavior; do not assume a join preserves row count.

theory.title: Transactions and concurrency
theory.explanation: Atomicity groups changes; isolation defines what concurrent transactions see. Locks and constraints coordinate conflicts. A correct design names the invariant and tests two interleaved sessions. Deadlock recovery must retry a safe unit of work, not a random final statement.
theory.workedExample: Two sessions decrementing stock via conditional arithmetic UPDATE serialize around the row and recheck the predicate instead of both trusting a stale read.
theory.pitfalls: Use the downloadable PostgreSQL practice schema, not your live training tables. Declare timestamp timezone and tie behavior; do not assume a join preserves row count.

theory.title: SQL indexing and plans
theory.explanation: Performance depends on data distribution, row counts, access patterns and the actual plan. An index is not automatically used or beneficial. Measure representative data, distinguish estimated from actual rows, and preserve correctness while changing query shape.
theory.workedExample: A filter on user_id ordered by created_at,id may benefit from a matching composite index; a broad full-table aggregate may correctly prefer a sequential scan.
theory.pitfalls: Use the downloadable PostgreSQL practice schema, not your live training tables. Declare timestamp timezone and tie behavior; do not assume a join preserves row count.

theory.title: Advanced PostgreSQL
theory.explanation: PostgreSQL supports recursive queries, JSONB, arrays and row-level security. These features solve specific data shapes but should not replace a clear relational model. Security policies must cover both rows visible before an update and rows permitted after it.
theory.workedExample: A recursive employee hierarchy starts from a manager and repeatedly joins employees.manager_id to the prior level, while preventing cycles in imperfect data.
theory.pitfalls: Use the downloadable PostgreSQL practice schema, not your live training tables. Declare timestamp timezone and tie behavior; do not assume a join preserves row count.

theory.title: Request routing and edge systems
theory.explanation: Routing controls how a request reaches a service, but different layers make different decisions. DNS routing, CDN edge selection, reverse proxying and application gateways are not interchangeable. Trace identity, timeouts and observability across each boundary.
theory.workedExample: For an authenticated API call, terminate TLS at a defined boundary, verify identity, authorize the resource, attach a request ID and bound the upstream deadline.
theory.pitfalls: State assumptions, label estimates, explain the first bottleneck and avoid promising exactly-once delivery or zero downtime without defining the boundary. Compare a simpler alternative.

theory.title: Storage and partitioning
theory.explanation: Storage design follows read/write patterns, consistency and growth. Replication improves availability only when the failover and acknowledgement contracts are explicit. Partitioning changes query costs and can concentrate load around poor keys.
theory.workedExample: Consistent hashing places keys and virtual nodes on a ring; adding a node moves a subset of ranges, but hot keys can remain hot regardless of average balance.
theory.pitfalls: State assumptions, label estimates, explain the first bottleneck and avoid promising exactly-once delivery or zero downtime without defining the boundary. Compare a simpler alternative.

theory.title: Consistency and concurrent workflows
theory.explanation: Consistency is a requirement, not a fashionable default. Some operations can tolerate stale reads; inventory, permissions or money may require stronger coordination. Model partial failure and retries before choosing a transaction or compensation approach.
theory.workedExample: A booking can atomically claim a unique seat and commit a reservation; payment is another boundary with idempotent retry and an explicit expiry/compensation policy.
theory.pitfalls: State assumptions, label estimates, explain the first bottleneck and avoid promising exactly-once delivery or zero downtime without defining the boundary. Compare a simpler alternative.

theory.title: Queues, events and workers
theory.explanation: Queues decouple acceptance from processing and buffer uneven workloads. Delivery semantics must be paired with consumer behavior. Retries, deduplication, ordering, poison messages and lag are product-visible concerns.
theory.workedExample: An outbox record committed with an order survives a publisher crash; a separate publisher retries it, while consumers deduplicate possible repeated deliveries.
theory.pitfalls: State assumptions, label estimates, explain the first bottleneck and avoid promising exactly-once delivery or zero downtime without defining the boundary. Compare a simpler alternative.

theory.title: Collaborative and social products
theory.explanation: User-facing systems need concrete journeys before infrastructure. Separate authoritative writes from derived feeds/search/counts. Permissions, abuse, fanout and offline behavior often change the design more than the basic CRUD endpoints.
theory.workedExample: A chat message has a durable ID and conversation sequence; delivery acknowledgments and read receipts are separate states, not one vague sent flag.
theory.pitfalls: State assumptions, label estimates, explain the first bottleneck and avoid promising exactly-once delivery or zero downtime without defining the boundary. Compare a simpler alternative.

theory.title: Commerce and booking systems
theory.explanation: Commerce workflows cross multiple failure and trust boundaries. Availability checks are not reservations; payment callbacks can repeat. State machines and durable operation identities make the differences between pending, confirmed, expired and compensated visible.
theory.workedExample: A shopping cart is editable intent. An order snapshots price and quantity; later catalog price changes should not silently rewrite historical purchases.
theory.pitfalls: State assumptions, label estimates, explain the first bottleneck and avoid promising exactly-once delivery or zero downtime without defining the boundary. Compare a simpler alternative.

theory.title: Infrastructure and resilience
theory.explanation: Resilience comes from bounded dependencies, clear health signals and tested recovery, not simply adding more replicas. Stateful scaling needs ownership transfer or shared durable state. Choose mechanisms against explicit failure scenarios and measure their cost.
theory.workedExample: A readiness check can remove an instance from traffic before termination; a bounded drain prevents existing requests from being cut off unnecessarily.
theory.pitfalls: State assumptions, label estimates, explain the first bottleneck and avoid promising exactly-once delivery or zero downtime without defining the boundary. Compare a simpler alternative.

theory.title: Search, analytics and observability
theory.explanation: Derived systems trade freshness for query efficiency. Define ingestion, indexing/aggregation, retention and correction paths. At scale, the important questions include duplicates, late data, schema evolution, hot partitions and the cost of replay.
theory.workedExample: Search indexes are derived views: a committed product update can precede searchable visibility, so define acceptable lag and a repair/reindex path.
theory.pitfalls: State assumptions, label estimates, explain the first bottleneck and avoid promising exactly-once delivery or zero downtime without defining the boundary. Compare a simpler alternative.

theory.title: Low-level design with OOP
theory.explanation: Low-level OOP design names responsibilities, invariants and collaboration contracts. Show interfaces and a concrete call sequence before drawing a large class hierarchy. Prefer composition where independent policies vary.
theory.workedExample: A parking system can separate AllocationStrategy from Ticket and PaymentGateway; capacity updates still need atomic coordination outside the object diagram.

theory.title: Low-level design without OOP
theory.explanation: A non-OOP design can express the same invariants with immutable records, pure transition functions and explicit I/O adapters. The goal is clear ownership and testable behavior, not banning every class in a dependency. Compare both approaches against the same requirements.
theory.workedExample: transition(state,event) can return {nextState,effects}; a separate runner performs effects and feeds confirmed outcomes back as events.
